scope: How exploratory testing is planned, run and reported so it finds what scripted tests miss and its results can be acted on: what a charter holds (mission, target areas, resources, the information sought, what to leave alone) and how one is written, how a session is bounded (time or step cap) and debriefed under session-based test management, and what each finding records (where it was seen, what was seen, what was expected, whether and how it repeats). Out of scope: authoring scripted end-to-end tests (e2e-test-authoring), triaging failing tests (test-failure-triage) and the issue tracker's own conventions (planning/project-management/issue-tracking); these are cited, not restated.
research_type: How-to / troubleshooting (intent Do; domain exploratory testing; method practitioner sources and published method guides). Product / how-to bar LOW-MEDIUM (broad independent consensus), no escalation. Session-length claims are metric claims and were scored on the Statistical bar; none of them rests on a study, so none meets it.

questions.text: Best practices: what is current best practice for this topic?
Known solutions: what solutions, patterns, libraries and tools already exist, and how do they compare?
Platform guidelines: what do the platform owners' own guidelines say, for each platform the topic touches (Apple, Android, Windows, web, the databases and runtimes concerned)?
The expert's view: if we hired an expert consultant in this topic, what would they tell us: what to do, what to avoid, and what people usually get wrong?

methodology.method: guidelines/researching/process/research-methodology-and-sources: orient and classify (how-to, exploratory testing), go to the standards and certification bodies first (ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-1 and -3, the ISTQB Foundation and Advanced Test Analyst syllabi) and the method owners (Jonathan Bach's session-based test management, James Bach's Heuristic Test Strategy Model, Hendrickson's Explore It!), then the platform owners' bug-reporting guidance (Apple, Android, Microsoft, Mozilla for the web) and practitioner and research sources (Rapid Software Testing, DevelopSense, Workroom Productions, the Association for Software Testing, Kaner, Whittaker, Ghazi et al.) for what no primary source covers; corroborate across independent publishers; record provenance at generation time.
methodology.search_strategy: WebSearch for charter templates and contents, session-based test management (session length, session sheets, debriefs, on-charter versus opportunity time), exploratory testing definitions in ISO 29119 and ISTQB, bug and incident report contents (expected and actual results, reproducibility, oracles), and the platform owners' bug-reporting pages; WebFetch or direct download of each page or PDF actually cited; arXiv and OpenAlex for empirical studies of charters.
methodology.inclusion: Standards and certification syllabi, method owners' own writing, platform owners' own guidance pages, practitioner writing by named authors with a long record in the field, and peer-reviewed or preprint research on test charters; each read in full or in the section quoted.
methodology.exclusion: Vendor marketing pages, anonymous blog posts, content farms, pages behind a paywall or login that could not be read (O'Reilly, Medium, Springer full text), and any page not fetched in this session.
methodology.scoring: guidelines/researching/evidence/verification-and-trust-scoring: Authority 30, Independent corroboration 25, Accuracy 20, Currency 10, Transparency 15; the how-to bar is LOW-MEDIUM (broad independent consensus); session-length claims take the Statistical bar. Independence is multi-independent only when two or more independent publishers hold the quoted words; every claim here quotes one publisher, so each is single, and corroboration across claims is noted in the trust basis.

summary: Exploratory testing is a recognised technique in ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-1 and the ISTQB syllabi: it designs, runs and evaluates tests together while learning the product, and hunts for hidden properties that formal techniques miss, which supports looking for what specs cannot anticipate. Under session-based test management a session is an uninterrupted, chartered, time-boxed block that is debriefed (PROOF) and recorded on a session sheet of notes, issues and bugs. The ISTQB Test Analyst syllabus, citing Ghazi et al., lists what a charter may hold (mission, duration, areas of interest, priorities, what will not be tested, limitations) and gives Hendrickson's 'Explore [target] With [resources] To discover [information]' format; Hendrickson warns against charters too specific or too broad. Defect-report guidance from ISTQB, Mozilla and Apple agrees on location, observed and expected results, steps and reproducibility, so the Worker Focus reporting rule, the observed-not-inferred check and the retry check hold. Four rules do not hold as written: no source bounds a session by a step count (every source uses a time box), no source speaks to staying on one origin, the Rapid Software Testing guide warns against a pedantic 'Expected:' line and asks for the oracle 'unless it is obvious' (contradicting the hard four-part fail), and session-based test management lets a tester divert to an off-charter problem and records it as opportunity time (contradicting 'out-of-charter rather than raised'). The ban on padding a clean session is unsupported; reporting what was and was not covered is supported. Apple, Android and Windows bear on the topic only through their bug-report guidance.
open_questions: Whether an automated session keeps a step cap at all, keeps it beside a time box, or replaces it with a time box as every source uses; and, if kept, what number (no source gives 25 or any step count).
Whether 'stay on the system under test's own origin' is kept as a safety or authorization policy of the house; no testing source states it, so it would rest on the owner's decision alone.

Whether an anomaly found outside the charter is raised as a finding and its time logged as opportunity (as session-based test management does) or only listed as out-of-charter (as the current Verify rule has it).
Whether the expectation stays a mandatory fourth part of every finding, or the finding must state its oracle only when the problem is not obvious, as the Rapid Software Testing guide advises.
Whether padding a clean session with severity-free observations stays a fail, given that session sheets and the HTSM quality story both keep notes and curios beside bugs.

Whether 'intermittent' requires one stated second attempt or a stated count of attempts and successes; Mozilla asks for 'at will, occasionally, or not at all' and more information when occasional, but no source fixes a number.
limitations: ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-1 and 29119-3 are paywalled; only the public previews hosted by iTeh Standards were read. The 29119-3 preview shows the incident report only in its table of contents, so the standard's own incident-report fields could not be quoted; ISTQB's defect-report list stands in for them.

O'Reilly and Medium refused automated fetches (HTTP 403), and chapter 2 of Hendrickson's Explore It! was not read in full; her charter template is cited through the ISTQB Test Analyst syllabus (primary) and Lyndsay's article (secondary), and her advice on good charters from the publisher's own excerpt.

Ghazi et al. (2017), which the ISTQB Test Analyst syllabus cites for charter contents, was read only as its arXiv abstract; its 35 content elements were not read in full. The Springer full texts of Afzal et al. (2014) and Itkonen and Mantyla (2014) on exploratory testing's effectiveness could not be read (login and bot protection), so no effectiveness figure is claimed.

No study backs any session length: the ninety minutes in session-based test management is one team's practice and Lyndsay's 10-120 minutes is a practitioner's range, so neither meets the Statistical bar, and no source at all gives a step count.
The Apple, Android and Mozilla bug-writing pages render with JavaScript and were read through WebFetch; the Mozilla page was read twice with consistent wording.
Windows and Apple platform owners publish nothing on exploratory charters or sessions; Microsoft's Azure Test Plans documentation covers a tool for exploratory sessions, not a method.
Kaner's definition is quoted from a slide whose bullets were joined into one sentence; the words are his, the bullet marks are dropped.
license: MIT (this research record); quoted material remains under its sources' terms and is quoted for verification.
